findings.paper_title: 26 09Sept24 512795 Initial Budget Estimate Nr 4 CB V2
findings.headline: Pupil referral unit cost estimate £16,999,519 with identified cost range of £16.5m to £17.5m due to volatile construction market
findings.detail: Stage 3 cost estimate for new two-storey pupil referral unit at Ash Grove, Radcliffe with total anticipated client cost of £16,999,519. The document identifies material cost uncertainty due to energy prices and geopolitical factors, with an anticipated range of £16.5m to £17.5m. The estimate includes £1,516,600 risk allowance and £627,700 inflation allowance, but explicitly notes that market supply prices are rising faster than forecast indices and these increases are not reflected in the estimate.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders need visibility of capital project cost risks. A £1 million range (6%) on a £17 million project represents material uncertainty, and the explicit note that actual market inflation may exceed forecast assumptions is material to forward financial planning and borrowing decisions.
findings.figures: Total anticipated cost £16,999,519; cost range £16.5m-£17.5m; construction cost £11,994,400; risk allowance £1,516,600; inflation allowance £627,700; assumed tender inflation 1.92%, construction inflation 1.88%
findings.quote: The construction market is very volatile at present and costs are unpredictable due to energy prices and the wars in Ukraine and Iran. We would anticipate that this scheme could cost between £16.5m and £17.5m

findings.paper_title: 9. Cabinet report - New Lease 6B 6C Bridge Trading Estate (Oct 2026)
findings.headline: Bury's Adult Care Equipment Service cost of £5.11 per resident is mid-range for Greater Manchester peer services (£3.88-£6.90 range)
findings.detail: The council compared operating costs across Greater Manchester councils. Costs range from £3.88 to £6.90 per head. Bury at £5.11 per head is in the middle of this distribution. The lowest-cost councils operate from wholly council-owned buildings with negligible property costs; only two services operate this way.
findings.matters: Shows the council's unit costs are not exceptional given the cost of the premises, and that cost differences between councils are largely property-driven rather than reflecting service efficiency.
findings.figures: Bury £5.11 per person; GM range £3.88-£6.90; two councils operate from council-owned buildings
findings.quote: the cost of delivering the service here in Bury is £5.11 per person compared to a low of £3.88 and a high of £6.90

findings.paper_title: 9. Cabinet report - New Lease 6B 6C Bridge Trading Estate (Oct 2026)
findings.headline: No readily available alternative premises identified; relocation estimated at £160k in dilapidation costs with service disruption risk
findings.detail: Alternatives were considered: relocating the service or closing it. Both were rejected. No suitable alternative premises have been identified. The existing unit has £436,925 of 2015 capital investment plus £18,000 lift installation. Relocation would incur approximately £160k in dilapidation and reinstatement works plus new fit-out costs.
findings.matters: The council's options are constrained by prior capital investment and lack of alternatives, effectively forcing acceptance of the rent increase to avoid larger one-time costs and service disruption to an essential social care function.
findings.figures: Capital investment 2015 £436,925; lift installation £18,000; estimated dilapidation £160k; unit 11,395 sq ft
findings.quote: there are no readily available alternative premises currently identified that would provide an equivalent operational base

findings.paper_title: 9. Cabinet report - New Lease 6B 6C Bridge Trading Estate (Oct 2026)
findings.headline: Agreed rent of £8.95 per sq ft is within local market range; market comparison shows £8.00-£10.00 typical for secondary industrial space
findings.detail: The council tested the new rent against comparable industrial accommodation in Bury and North Manchester. Secondary industrial space typically ranges £8.00-£10.00 per sq ft; newer or higher specification premises exceed £11.00 per sq ft. The agreed rate is positioned at the lower end of that range.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the substantial cost increase reflects current market conditions rather than a punitive negotiated outcome, though it confirms the council has limited negotiating leverage.
findings.figures: Agreed £8.95 per sq ft; local market £8.00-£10.00; higher specification >£11.00 per sq ft; unit 1,058.69 sq m
findings.quote: The agreed rent of approximately £8.95 per sq ft is therefore considered to be within the range evidenced by the local market.

findings.paper_title: 9. Cabinet report - New Lease 6B 6C Bridge Trading Estate (Oct 2026)
findings.headline: Open market rent review on 18 May 2030 creates further cost uncertainty; same date as tenant-only break clause
findings.detail: The lease includes an open market rent review on 18 May 2030 when the rent will reset to the greater of the passing rent (£102,000) or the open market value. The council's break option (six months' notice required) is dated 17 May 2030, meaning the council's exit decision point coincides with potential for a further rent increase.
findings.matters: Creates material future cost uncertainty; market rent reviews typically increase with inflation, and the council's mitigation options converge at a single point five years into the lease.
findings.figures: Rent review and break clause both due May 2030; basis is greater of passing rent or open market rent
findings.quote: Rent review: open market rent review on 18 May 2030, with the reviewed rent being the greater of the passing rent or the open market rent determined in accordance with the lease.

findings.paper_title: 9. Cabinet report - New Lease 6B 6C Bridge Trading Estate (Oct 2026)
findings.headline: Annual recurring lease cost increasing by £44,210 to £102,000 per annum from May 2025, creating a material MTFS pressure
findings.detail: The council is renewing its lease for units 6b and 6c Bridge Trading Estate to maintain Adult Care Equipment Services. Rent increases from £57,790 to £102,000 per annum—a £44,210 annual recurrent cost pressure. The 10-year lease runs from 18 May 2025 to 17 May 2035, representing a committed £1m+ expenditure over its term.
findings.matters: A material new recurring revenue commitment that requires budget accommodation in the medium-term financial strategy and cannot easily be reversed because the service is essential.
findings.figures: £102,000 per annum vs previous £57,790; £44,210 annual increase; 10-year term to May 2035
findings.quote: There is an annual recurrent cost pressure of £44,210 relating to the new lease which will be reflected in the updated medium term financial strategy

findings.headline: External funding carries mandatory spending deadlines; failure to approve programmes risks delaying delivery and losing available investment within required periods
findings.detail: The report flags that external funding carries mandatory spending conditions and deadlines. Without Cabinet approval, the council 'risks delaying delivery, affecting spend profiles and reducing the Council's ability to maximise the benefits of available investment within the required funding periods'. This underscores the urgency of programme approvals in accessing external funding and the risk of forfeiting allocations if they are not deployed by required dates.
findings.matters: External funding deadlines create a real financial risk: councils can lose allocations if unable to commit and spend by prescribed timescales. Understanding the stringency of these conditions is material to assess a council's capital delivery capacity.
findings.figures: No specific figures
findings.quote: Failure to commit funding through an approved programme risks delaying delivery, affecting spend profiles and reducing the Council's ability to maximise the benefits of available investment within the required funding periods.

findings.headline: Cabinet approves £12.917 million highways capital programme for 2026/27, with spending extending into 2027/28
findings.detail: The programme allocates investment across multiple asset types: resurfacing carriageways (£6.585m), preventative carriageways (£1.368m), structures (£1.160m), routine maintenance (£1.253m), footways (£1.000m), road safety (£1.113m), street lighting (£167k), drainage repairs (£220k) and rights of way (£50k). Delivery timescale extends into 2027/28 to support 'effective programme management' and coordination with other investment. Investment is prioritised using a risk-based asset management approach based on condition, safety and network need.
findings.matters: Capital programme decisions show how councils sequence major asset investment; the phased delivery and multi-category approach illustrates asset management maturity and strategic coordination of infrastructure spending.
findings.figures: Total £12.917m; Resurfacing £6.585m; Preventative maintenance £1.368m; Structures £1.160m; Routine maintenance £1.253m; Footways £1.000m; Road safety £1.113m; Street lighting £167k; Drainage £220k; Rights of way £50k
findings.quote: The Highways Capital Investment Programme sets out how £12.917m of available funding will be invested to maintain and improve one of the Council's most important public assets. Funding has been secured through a combination of CRSTS, ITB, Network North and the additional £4.374m Mayor's Pothole Fund allocation

findings.headline: Mayor's Pothole Fund allocated £4.374 million to Bury for highway maintenance and improvements
findings.detail: Bury has received £4.374 million from the Mayor's Pothole Fund as part of the 2026/27 funding package. This is described as 'a significant investment' providing 'an opportunity to accelerate improvements in network condition and resilience'. It represents the largest single funding source in the programme, combining with CRSTS (£7.317m), Integrated Transport Block (£1.113m) and Network North (£113k) to reach the total £12.917m investment.
findings.matters: External funding is central to council capital strategies; securing additional sources beyond core government allocations enables accelerated investment and demonstrates competitive success in accessing available resources—a pattern other councils monitor.
findings.figures: £4.374 million
findings.quote: The programme is supported by a number of funding streams, including the recently announced £4.374 million allocation from the Mayor's Pothole Fund. This represents a significant investment in Bury's highway infrastructure and provides an opportunity to accelerate improvements in network condition and resilience.

findings.headline: Budget gap for 2027/28 has increased by £6.434m (from £13.898m to £20.332m) since the February 2026 budget was approved, primarily due to £4.084m of demand and volume growth.
findings.detail: Departments have refreshed budget assumptions following the 2026/27 Quarter One monitoring. The largest movements are: demand/volume growth £4.084m, Real Living Wage increase £1.482m (6.4%), and treasury/capital financing £3.094m. These increases have been partially offset by savings proposals, but reflect the pace at which cost and demand growth is outpacing the council's ability to find offsets.
findings.matters: A budget gap that has grown by 46% in eight months (February to October 2026) signals deteriorating financial sustainability and forecasting uncertainty. If demand continues to grow faster than assumed, the 2027/28 gap could further widen beyond the £9.585m forecast.
findings.figures: February 2026 gap £13.898m; October 2026 gap £20.332m; increase £6.434m; demand growth £4.084m; Real Living Wage £1.482m
findings.quote: Since the approval of the February 2026 budget, the Council has undertaken a comprehensive review of its budget assumptions... the 2027/28 budget gap has a net increase of £6.434m, comprising of an increase in budget assumptions of £6.161m and a decrease in expected funding of £0.273m.

findings.headline: Health and Adult Care and Children and Young People together represent 65% of the net budget (£172.615m of £264.520m in 2027/28), reflecting sustained demand and cost growth in social care.
findings.detail: These two services account for the largest proportion of council expenditure and are forecast to grow faster than other services due to rising demand, increasing complexity of need, and market cost pressures. The budget assumptions include a Real Living Wage increase of 6.4% for 2027/28, impacting primarily adult social care fee levels. Both services are overspending in 2026/27, indicating baseline demand pressures are embedded in the budget.
findings.matters: The concentration of spending in demand-led social care services means the council has limited discretion over expenditure. Demand growth, demographic change, and care market costs are largely outside council control. A council where two-thirds of spending is in volatile, demand-led services faces higher financial risk.
findings.figures: Health and Adult Care £103.992m (39% of net budget); Children and Young People £68.623m (26%); combined £172.615m (65%); Real Living Wage assumption 6.4%
findings.quote: Health and Adult Care and Children and Young People continue to account for the largest proportion of Council expenditure. Together, these services represent £172.615m of the proposed 2027/28 net budget, approximately 65% of total expenditure, reflecting sustained demand growth, increasing complexity of need and ongoing market cost pressures across social care services.

findings.headline: Policy savings of £2.686m requiring public consultation include removal of homecare charging cap (£0.700m), leisure income increases (£1.002m), and green waste charging (£0.612m).
findings.detail: These proposals are subject to public consultation between 19 October and 30 November 2026. The removal of the homecare charging cap affects 38 residents (average age 81) and would increase their care charges by an average of £380 per week. Leisure fees would rise 20% annually for two years (2027/28-2028/29) to bring charges closer to market rates. Green waste charging would introduce a new charge from 2028/29.
findings.matters: Policy savings are subject to community and stakeholder pushback, and may not be fully delivered. If consultation leads to removal or reduction of proposals, the gap widens. These savings are modest in scale relative to the total gap, indicating the bulk of the budget challenge is demand and cost-driven, not driven by unaffordable current-year policies.
findings.figures: £2.686m total policy savings (£1.070m in 2027/28); removal of homecare cap £0.700m; leisure income £1.002m; green waste charging £0.612m; consultation period 19 October - 30 November 2026
findings.quote: Of the £17.451m total new savings, £14.765m relates to non-policy decisions... whilst £2.686m requires a policy decision and formal consultation prior to implementation.

findings.headline: Total savings programme of £27.251m includes £5.480m of workforce reductions, with voluntary exit scheme in progress and compulsory redundancy not ruled out.
findings.detail: The savings comprise £9.800m of previously approved savings and £17.451m of new proposals. Of the new proposals, £14.765m are non-policy decisions (vacancy deletion, staffing restructuring) and £2.686m require policy decisions through consultation. Workforce savings represent a target of approximately 5% of gross staffing budget through vacancy deletion and reorganisation. The council has launched a voluntary exit scheme but notes that compulsory redundancy may be required if further savings are identified.
findings.matters: Workforce savings of this scale carry delivery risk: labour markets, service continuity, and council capacity to redesign services. The note that compulsory redundancy cannot be ruled out signals that the council expects further savings requirements beyond those currently identified.
findings.figures: £27.251m total savings (2027/28-2029/30); £5.480m workforce savings; approximately 5% of gross staffing budget; £17.560m in 2027/28 alone
findings.quote: Current MTFS assumptions include recurring workforce savings of £5.480m through vacancy deletion and related measures... the Council will continue to explor e opportunities to surpass this target... the Council cannot rule out the possibility of compulsory redundancies being required.

findings.headline: 2026/27 Quarter One forecast overspend of £5.691m (2.26% of budget) concentrated in social care, driven by ongoing demand and market cost pressures.
findings.detail: Health and Adult Care shows a £2.543m overspend, Children and Young People £2.212m, and Corporate Core £2.131m, collectively accounting for £6.886m of the total £5.691m forecast outturn variance. The overspend reflects increasing demand, rising care placement costs, and workforce pressures. This in-year position directly worsens the reserves position and informs the 2027/28 budget setting.
findings.matters: In-year overspends are recurring. If demand-led pressures are crystallising in 2026/27, they form the baseline for 2027/28 budget assumptions. An overspend that requires reserve drawdown reduces the buffer available for 2027/28 and signals that the structural underlying cost is higher than anticipated.
findings.figures: Total net revenue budget £252.135m; Quarter One forecast outturn £257.826m; variance £5.691m (2.26%)
findings.quote: The forecast overspend is largely concentrated within services that are experiencing significant demand-led and workforce related pressures.

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves have depleted by £87.477m (66%) from £131.583m in March 2020 to £44.106m in March 2026.
findings.detail: The chart in the paper documents the sustained drawdown of reserves over six years to support budget delivery and manage in-year pressures. The rate of depletion significantly exceeds the pace at which reserves are being replenished, demonstrating that reserve balances are being consumed faster than they can be rebuilt.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion at this rate is unsustainable. A council reaching the end of its reserve buffer faces a cliff edge where it can no longer absorb unexpected pressures or timing mismatches between spending and income without accessing external support or unplanned service cuts.
findings.figures: £131.583m (March 2020) to £44.106m (March 2026); reduction of £87.477m; average annual reduction of £14.6m
findings.quote: Whilst reserves have enabled the Council to manage exceptional financial challenges over recent years, the scale of the reduction demonstrates that reserve balances are being depleted at a significantly faster rate than they can be replenished. This trend is not sustainable over the medium term.

findings.headline: Budget Stabilisation Reserve forecast to fall to £5.977m at March 2027, insufficient to cover the £9.585m budget gap.
findings.detail: The primary reserve used to support budget sustainability is forecast to reduce from £15.599m at March 2026 to £5.977m at March 2027. This follows an approved use of £3.977m in 2026/27 and a further estimated £5.691m contribution to offset the Quarter One forecast overspend. The reserve balance remaining is below the size of the 2027/28 budget gap.
findings.matters: The council has historically relied on reserves to balance budgets while savings are delivered. Once reserves fall below the annual budget gap, the council cannot close deficits through this mechanism and must deliver recurring savings or access external support.
findings.figures: Opening balance £15.599m; approved use £3.977m; forecast contribution £5.691m; closing forecast £5.977m; against 2027/28 gap of £9.585m
findings.quote: The Council no longer has a sufficient Budget Stabilisation Reserve to fund the current budget gaps and therefore cannot rely upon reserves as a viable means of balancing future budgets.

findings.headline: Residual budget gap of £9.585m remains for 2027/28 even after proposed savings of £10.747m, rising to cumulative gap of £17.508m by 2029/30.
findings.detail: The council identified a budget gap of £20.332m for 2027/28 before applying savings. Despite proposing £10.747m of new savings, primarily through vacancy deletion, service redesign, and policy changes, a shortfall of £9.585m persists. This reflects sustained demand growth in social care, inflation pressures, and capital financing costs that savings proposals have not fully closed.
findings.matters: A residual funding gap this large, unmatched by reserves, indicates the council cannot set a balanced budget from its own resources and must either find further savings, increase council tax beyond referendum limits, access Exceptional Financial Support, or draw down reserves unsustainably.
findings.figures: £20.332m opening gap; £10.747m new savings identified; £9.585m residual gap; cumulative £17.508m gap by 2029/30
findings.quote: Notwithstanding savings proposals totalling £10.747m, a budget gap of £9.585m remains in 2027/28, increasing to a cumulative gap of £17.508m by 2029/30.

findings.headline: Eagle & Child Retaining Wall project £460,000 deferred to 2027/28 pending legal easement agreement with brewery
findings.detail: Recent inspections identified bulging and defects to a retaining wall requiring investigative works and masonry repairs. The project is programmed for 2027/28 at £460,000 with no expenditure in 2026/27 because the start on site is dependent on resolving a legal easement with the brewery.
findings.matters: A material portion of the 2027/28 capital programme (40% of the two-year total) is contingent on completing third-party legal agreements, creating execution risk on work identified by inspection as necessary.
findings.figures: £460,000 (2027/28 only); total programme £1,160,000 across both years
findings.quote: Start on site has been delayed whilst a legal easement is agreed with the brewery

findings.paper_title: Pyramid Park and Q-Park Disposal - Cabinet Report - Part A (1)
findings.headline: Disposal will reduce revenue costs of holding long-term vacant sites, but ongoing annual cost is not quantified
findings.detail: The council has been bearing revenue costs to maintain, hold and secure Pyramid Park (7.4 acres vacant for over 15 years) and Q-Park (1 acre vacant since 2009). The paper states that disposal will reduce these revenue costs, but does not quantify the current annual costs or the expected savings from disposal, making it impossible to assess the materiality of this revenue benefit.
findings.matters: Ongoing costs to hold derelict sites represent a drag on the council's revenue budget; the actual size of this saving is not disclosed.
findings.figures: Pyramid Park: 7.4 acres, vacant over 15 years; Q-Park: 1 acre, vacant since 2009; annual holding costs not specified
findings.quote: reduce the revenue costs of holding, maintaining and securing these long-term vacant, town centre opportunity sites

findings.paper_title: Pyramid Park and Q-Park Disposal - Cabinet Report - Part A (1)
findings.headline: Q-Park has multiple existing leasehold interests with incomplete title clarity, risking disposal delays
findings.detail: Q-Park site is subject to six leases including three occupational leases held by Q-Park Ltd (car park operator), NHS Property Services Limited, and Six Town Housing Limited. The council has not completed title due diligence, noting that a title review will be undertaken as soon as possible to identify all third-party rights. These leasehold interests may affect the timing of the proposed development, with potential to delay financial completion and threaten the 31 March 2027 grant deadline.
findings.matters: Incomplete title certainty and multiple occupational leases create legal and timing risks that could delay the development, push past the BLRF2 deadline, and jeopardise the £1.73m grant.
findings.figures: Six leases affecting Q-Park site, three occupational leases identified
findings.quote: It is understood that there are six leases affecting the site, including three apparent occupational leases. Given the wider leasehold structure, a title review will be undertaken as soon as possible

findings.paper_title: Pyramid Park and Q-Park Disposal - Cabinet Report - Part A (1)
findings.headline: Section 106 planning obligations will reduce the net capital receipt from disposal, but amount is not disclosed
findings.detail: The paper acknowledges that planning obligations will impact the land value received but does not quantify these obligations. Section 106 contributions can be substantial, meaning the actual capital receipt to the council will be lower than the red book valuation. The decision on final disposal terms and capital receipt has been delegated to executives specifically because of this uncertainty.
findings.matters: Unquantified Section 106 obligations represent downside to the financial case made for this disposal and create uncertainty about the actual benefit to the council's finances.
findings.figures: Amount of Section 106 contributions not specified in Part A
findings.quote: the eventual land offer is likely to be impacted by Section 106 contributions obligated through the planning approval process

findings.paper_title: Pyramid Park and Q-Park Disposal - Cabinet Report - Part A (1)
findings.headline: £1.73m BLRF2 grant faces full clawback if disposal milestone of 31 March 2027 is missed
findings.detail: The council received £1.73m in BLRF2 grant funding conditional on disposing Pyramid Park to a developer by 31 March 2027 and having new homes completed by 31 March 2029. The paper explicitly warns that failure to meet these milestones creates a risk of grant clawback. Remediation works are underway with autumn 2026 completion expected, leaving a tight timeline to secure developer completion and financial closure by March 2027.
findings.matters: A £1.73m clawback would be material to the council's financial position and would also jeopardise the anticipated capital receipt, creating a double-hit to their balance sheet and budget.
findings.figures: £1.73 million grant funding, disposal deadline 31 March 2027, homes completion deadline 31 March 2029, remediation completion autumn 2026
findings.quote: This risks a full grant claw back of the £1.73 million brownfield funding provided by One Public Estate (OPE)

findings.headline: Treasury investment balances fell 29% to £14.6m, reducing financial flexibility and internal borrowing capacity
findings.detail: Council's treasury investments declined from £20.7m to £14.6m (£6.1m reduction), representing all surplus cash and reserves. Cash now represents only 4% of gross borrowing compared to 7% previously, indicating council is increasingly externally financed and has limited capacity to internally self-manage cash flows.
findings.matters: Significantly reduces council's buffer to absorb timing differences between income and expenditure; increases dependence on external debt markets; limits ability to avoid external borrowing through internal resource management
findings.figures: Treasury investments £20.7m to £14.618m (reduction £6.082m, -29%); cash as % of gross borrowing declined from 7.0% to 4.0%
findings.quote: As of 31 March 2026, the council held £14.618m of invested funds, representing income received in advance of expenditure plus balances and reserves held

findings.headline: PWLB refinancing in November 2025 realised £13.61m discount; £1.36m benefit in 2025/26
findings.detail: Council rescheduled selected PWLB loans following treasury adviser advice, achieving £13.61m total discount on early repayments and replacement borrowing. Savings recognised over 10 years; 2025/26 benefit £1.361m. Demonstrates active treasury management but refinancing activity indicates some debt was being opportunistically restructured.
findings.matters: Shows competent debt cost management reducing interest burden; but refinancing suggests structured opportunity cost optimisation rather than passive holding
findings.figures: £13.61m total discount; £1.361m 2025/26 savings
findings.quote: This approach has resulted in an overall improvement in the Authority's borrowing position with an overall discount achieved of £13.61m which will be recognised annually over the next 10 years. The savings recognised in 2025/26 equates to £1.361m

findings.headline: Gross borrowing increased £70.4m to £365.7m; Capital Financing Requirement up £44.9m
findings.detail: Council's external debt increased from £295.3m to £365.7m during 2025/26 to support capital expenditure of £100.4m. Underlying CFR rose £44.9m to £447.5m, indicating continued reliance on external borrowing rather than internal resources to finance capital programmes.
findings.matters: Council is borrowing at scale to fund capital; demonstrates sustained capital-driven borrowing need; increases annual interest cost burden on revenue; indicates continued debt-market dependence
findings.figures: Gross borrowing £295.266m to £365.671m (increase £70.405m); CFR £402.572m to £447.529m (increase £44.957m); capital expenditure £100.413m
findings.quote: On 31st March 2026, the Council held £365.673m of loans, an increase of £70.404m on the previous year as part of its strategy for funding previous and current years' capital programmes

findings.headline: Debt maturity profile concentrated in near-term; proportion due within 12 months doubled to 17.5%
findings.detail: Fixed-rate debt maturing under 12 months jumped from £24.9m (8.4%) to £64.1m (17.5%), while debt maturing in 10+ years fell from £129.8m (44%) to £73.5m (20%). The council faces £64m of refinancing risk in 2026/27, concentrated in a single year when interest rates remain elevated.
findings.matters: Refinancing £64m at current PWLB rates (10-year at 5.92% vs council's 3.50% average) will materially increase annual interest costs; concentration of refinancing risk in single year reduces flexibility
findings.quote: The maturity structure of the debt portfolio was as follows: [Table 5 showing 2025/26 under 12 months £64.072m at 17.52% versus 2024/25 £24.868m at 8.42%]

findings.headline: £4.294m of savings from 2025/26 carried forward as unachieved, including £1.610m Housing integration saving unmet in 2026/27 despite two years of effort
findings.detail: The council failed to deliver £4.294m of planned savings in 2025/26 and rolled them forward into 2026/27. Of these, £1.610m Housing integration savings remain unmet. The paper notes this 'represents a recurring pressure from 2025/26 where the saving was not delivered and remains unmet in 2026/27.' The council is attempting delivery through HRA/General Fund cost reviews, but states: 'Any element of the saving that is then assessed as being undeliverable would then be reflected in the MTFS'—effectively an admission that the saving may never materialise.
findings.matters: When a large saving (£1.6m) fails to deliver two years running, it signals either structural inability to change the cost/service model or poor governance; unachieved savings are often the first sign of broader budget crises
findings.figures: Unachieved 2025/26 savings carried forward £4.294m; Housing integration unmet £1.610m; Unit 4 reimplementation delayed to April 2027 (£0.753m); total carried-forward risk £2.363m (£1.610m + £0.753m)
findings.quote: this represents a recurring pressure from 2025/26 where the saving was not delivered and remains unmet in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Agency staffing costs overrunning by £5.862m (budgeted £1.925m, forecast £7.786m), indicating workforce restructures are delayed and control over staffing spend is lost
findings.detail: Strategy & Transformation alone is forecasting £3.324m agency overspend against £0.220m budget. The council is attempting mitigation through £2.000m recruitment delays, yielding only a net £0.035m favourable variance across all staffing. Multiple services note interim and locum staffing 'pending implementation' of restructures, suggesting organisational change initiatives are running behind, forcing reliance on expensive temporary labour. This is a direct consequence of unachieved savings.
findings.matters: High agency costs indicate lost control of a discretionary cost; they are typically 20–40% more expensive than permanent staff and are hard to reverse once vendors are embedded, reducing management optionality
findings.figures: Budgeted agency spend £1.925m; forecast £7.786m (£5.862m, 305% overspend); Strategy & Transformation agency variance £3.324m; partial offset from recruitment delays £2.000m
findings.quote: the £5.897m favourable variance on staffing budgets is offset by a forecast overspend on agency costs of £5.862m, resulting in a net favourable variance of £0.035m across staffing and agency budgets.

findings.headline: Capital programme expanded 20% to £132.440m at Q1 but acknowledged as 'very ambitious' and under review for deliverability; only 14% spent by end June
findings.detail: Approved programme (Feb 2026): £110.212m. Q1 additions: £17.336m slippage, £7.311m new schemes, less £2.419m rephasing = net £22.228m increase to £132.440m. The paper states: 'It is recognised that this represents a very ambitious programme and is being reviewed currently to provide assurance on deliverability and expected outcomes and the result of the review and any reprofiling will be included as part of the Quarter 2 report.' By 30 June, only £18.5m (14%) had been spent, raising questions about full-year delivery and whether forecasts are realistic.
findings.matters: When councils expand capital programmes mid-year and then concurrently acknowledge 'ambition' risk and commit to mid-year reviews, it signals either poor initial planning or slippage pressure; missed capital delivery frees up cash but also suggests projects are at risk
findings.figures: Programme revised from £110.212m to £132.440m (net increase £22.228m); Q1 spend £18.500m of £132.440m (14% by 30 June)
findings.quote: It is recognised that this represents a very ambitious programme and is being reviewed currently to provide assurance on deliverability and expected outcomes and the result of the review and any reprofiling will be included as part of the Quarter 2 report.

findings.headline: Treasury borrowing costs forecasting £1.015m pressure from loan refinancing at higher interest rates, compounded by new borrowing for capital programmes
findings.detail: The council is refinancing maturing debt in a higher interest rate environment. The paper states: 'the requirement to undertake further borrowing to support delivery of the approved capital programme has increased financing costs and contributed to the forecast overspend.' The council is now proposing an additional £0.350m General Fund prudential borrowing and £0.210m HRA prudential borrowing, which will increase debt service costs into 2027/28 and beyond. With revenue already under pressure, higher debt service reduces capacity for services.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether a council can service debt; rising interest costs on a static revenue base indicate declining debt service coverage and higher default risk if revenue pressures persist
findings.figures: Treasury Management forecast pressure £1.015m; additional General Fund prudential borrowing proposed £0.350m; additional HRA prudential borrowing £0.210m; total borrowing now £38.48m General Fund (was £30.361m)
findings.quote: forecast pressure of £1.015m relating to increased borrowing costs. This pressure reflects the refinancing of maturing loans during 2026/27 at higher interest rates, driven by the prevailing interest rate environment. In addition, the requirement to undertake further borrowing to support delivery of the approved capital programme has increased financing costs and contributed to the forecast overspend.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block cumulative deficit reaching £11.416m by March 2027 despite £19.157m Stability Grant, reflecting structural SEND cost growth
findings.detail: The High Needs allocation is £53.582m; forecast expenditure is £65.350m—an £11.768m gap. Even with a £19.157m government Stability Grant (90% of eligible deficit), the council carries forward an £11.416m deficit to 2027/28. This signals that SEND costs are outpacing both the allocation and government support. The council notes deficits are 'building over a number of years' due to allocation freezes, rising pupil SEN proportions, and expansion to 19–25-year-olds without funding.
findings.matters: DSG deficits are technical (unusable reserves) but foreshadow General Fund transfers; Bury's £11.4m forward deficit means future revenue budgets will face pressure to bridge it, further reducing financial flexibility
findings.figures: HNB allocation £53.582m; forecast spend £65.350m; in-year deficit £10.287m; brought-forward deficit 2025/26 £20.285m; forecast forward deficit 2027/28 £11.416m; Stability Grant (partial) £19.157m
findings.quote: The forecast 2026/27 DSG deficit position is £10.287m.

findings.headline: Collection Fund forecast £6.148m deficit (Bury's share £5.571m) with Council Tax collection rate falling below 98% target as cost-of-living pressures mount
findings.detail: The forecast combines £2.223m brought forward from 2025/26 with a new £3.924m in-year deficit. Council Tax collection is forecast to fall below the 98% target due to cost-of-living pressures on residents. Impairment allowance for Council Tax arrears increased £3.061m, reflecting expected non-payment. Historical collection rates (95.26% in 2025/26, 95.59% in 2024/25) show the council is already underperforming its 98% target, and the trajectory is worsening.
findings.matters: Council Tax and Business Rates are the second-largest funding stream (£234m budgeted); a 2–3% decline in collection means £4.7m–7m lost annually, and rising arrears signal household stress that may persist
findings.figures: Collection Fund forecast deficit £6.148m (Bury share £5.571m); in-year deficit £3.924m; brought-forward deficit £2.223m; Council Tax impairment allowance increase £3.061m; actual collection rates 2025/26: 95.26%, 2024/25: 95.59%
findings.quote: The current in year collection for Council Tax is forecast to fall below the budgeted collection rate of 98%, largely due to the cost-of-living pressures affecting residents.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care community care packages repeating a £6m overspend from 2025/26, indicating the overspend is structural, not one-off
findings.detail: Care in the Community is £2.624m over budget (4.02%) across Supporting Living, Nursing Homes, Direct Payments, and Domiciliary care. The paper states explicitly: 'The pressure on Care packages in 2026/27 is a continuation of the £6m overspend on community care packages in 2025/26.' This is a second consecutive year of the same pressure, suggesting budget assumptions about demand or unit costs are systematically wrong and the council has not corrected them.
findings.matters: Recurring overspends indicate that budget setting is detached from reality; when a £6m overspend repeats, it signals the budget planning process is broken and councils typically respond by drawing reserves until they run out
findings.figures: 2026/27 Care in Community overspend £2.624m (4.02%); continuation of £6.000m overspend from 2025/26
findings.quote: The pressure on Care packages in 2026/27 is a continuation of the £6m overspend on community care packages in 2025/26.

findings.headline: Children's residential and fostering placements overrunning by £2.938m total due to 10.2% price inflation and volume growth, with complex cases showing no containment
findings.detail: Residential placements overspent by £1.912m (11.8%) due to £1.724m price increase at 10.2% inflation and volume increases. Independent Fostering Agency placements overspent £1.026m (24.1%) due to 12 more placements than budgeted and 'significantly increased' prices. Despite 'additional growth added to the 2026/27 budget to meet demand, inflation and price increases, the service is still reporting a significant pressure.' The directorate notes 'further challenges are anticipated this financial year' and plans 'detailed intensive oversight'—meaning the cost spiral is not contained.
findings.matters: Double-digit annual price inflation on an already-expensive service (residential placements are typically £3k–5k per week) signals a market supply crisis that no council controls, making future costs unpredictable and further reserve drawdowns likely
findings.figures: Residential placements £1.912m overspend (11.8% of £17.2m budget); price inflation 10.2%; Independent Fostering £1.026m overspend (24.1% of £4.3m budget); 12 additional placements vs. budget
findings.quote: Children's residential placements including Children with Disabilities has a forecast adverse variance of £1.912m (11.8%). This is largely driven by an estimated £1.724m increase in costs in relation to increased average prices (10.2%)

findings.headline: £5.691m revenue overspend in Q1 (2.26% of £252m budget) with only 88.85% of £20.860m total savings forecast to deliver; £2.326m shortfall unmet
findings.detail: The council required £20.860m in total savings (including £4.294m carried forward from 2025/26). At Q1, only £15.696m from original plans and £2.838m from mitigations are forecast to deliver, totalling £18.534m. This leaves £2.326m unmet—74.6% of it (£1.735m) in Children and Young People. The paper describes work 'continuing to both identify further in-year mitigations and bring forward the delivery of approved savings that are currently assessed as being delayed' but gives no schedule for recovery.
findings.matters: When a council delivers less than 89% of a full budget savings programme, the structural gap is larger than acknowledged, and future years' budgets will face the same problem unless the underlying cost base or service model changes fundamentally
findings.figures: Total savings requirement £20.860m; forecast delivery £18.534m (88.85%); shortfall £2.326m (11.15%); CYP directorate shortfall £1.735m (74.6% of total)

findings.headline: Budget Stabilisation Reserve forecast to fall from £15.599m to £5.977m (61% decline); General Fund reserves declining from £90.414m (2024) to £32.059m (2027)
findings.detail: Starting balance March 2026 was £15.599m. The approved budget drew £3.977m. The Q1 £5.691m overspend would require a further £5.691m draw, leaving just £5.977m. The position is unsustainable.' Total General Fund reserves are forecast to fall from £44.106m to £32.059m (27.3% reduction in one year), continuing a three-year depletion from £90.414m (2024) to £32.059m (2027).
findings.matters: A lender's credit assessment depends on the council's capacity to absorb shocks or revenue shortfalls; when reserves are depleted on this trajectory, the council has no buffer left and becomes entirely dependent on grant income or external borrowing to manage volatility
findings.figures: Budget Stabilisation Reserve: £15.599m (31 Mar 2026) → £5.977m forecast (31 Mar 2027); GF reserves: £44.106m → £32.059m; three-year depletion: £90.414m (2024) → £32.059m (2027)
findings.quote: the current forecast overspend of £5.691m would reduce the balance on the Budget Stabilisation Reserve to £5.977m. findings.matters: Non-compliance with statutory Decent Homes Standard represents a regulatory and housing quality risk; a lender would assess whether planned capital spend is sufficient to resolve this backlog.

findings.headline: Council manages debt above its calculated liability benchmark through active drawdown of balance sheet reserves to minimize interest costs.
findings.detail: Existing borrowing of £365.671m currently exceeds the calculated liability benchmark of £361.100m. The council deliberately maintains this position by using cash-backed reserves rather than borrowing the full Capital Financing Requirement of £437.2m. As reserves deplete, the council will be forced to increase external borrowing to the benchmark level and beyond.
findings.matters: Councils using reserves to offset borrowing are managing down their reserve balances. This implies finite depletion and eventual upward pressure on borrowing, which lenders need to monitor as an indicator of the council's future debt trajectory and financial stress.
findings.figures: Existing borrowing £365.671m; Liability benchmark £361.100m; Loans CFR £437.200m
findings.quote: These balances improve the Council's cash position and enable it to maintain an under-borrowed position by not externally borrowing up to the full CFR, thus saving on interest costs.

findings.matters: Growing CFR indicates expanding underlying debt levels and reduced financial flexibility. Lenders track CFR growth as an indicator of whether capital programmes are sustainable and whether the council's debt trajectory is manageable.

findings.headline: Disclaimer opinions on financial statements for four consecutive years (2022–2025), meaning auditors cannot give assurance on the accounts.

findings.headline: Multiple demand-led service pressures in Children's, Adult Social Care, SEND and Dedicated Schools Grant offsetting savings efforts
findings.detail: The Finance Board tracked 'delivery of savings and reviewed financial pressures, including demand-led pressures in Children's Services, Adult Social Care, SEND and the Dedicated Schools Grant' (section 8.5 summary). If birth rates, aging populations, or complexity of need increase faster than resources, the council faces recurring budget shortfalls that zero-based budgeting cannot solve. This is a structural financial sustainability risk.

findings.headline: Existing financial management system at end of lifecycle with inherent risks, manual processes and compliance concerns
findings.detail: The council notes its current Financial Management System is 'nearing the end of its lifecycle' and carries 'inherent risks and compliance concerns' (section 6.6-6.7). The system is characterised by 'fragmented financial processes, reliance on manual tasks, an over-complicated coding structure and a lack of self-service options'. These issues are 'affecting the efficiency of the finance service and the wider organisation'. The council is undertaking a Unit4 system replacement project, but this work is ongoing and system risks persist.
findings.matters: Aging financial systems with high manual reliance create operational risk (errors, delays, fraud) and prevent timely financial reporting. Compliance concerns in the existing system could indicate breaches of financial controls or regulatory requirements. System replacement projects are high-risk; if Unit4 implementation stumbles, financial visibility and control will worsen.

findings.headline: Structural funding gap requires zero-based budgeting of all council services with explicit goal of ending reserve dependency

The explicit goal was to identify 'proposals that will enable a balanced budget to be set without recourse to reserves over the current medium term financial strategy'. This signals the council has identified a permanent, structural mismatch between its income and its spending commitments.
findings.matters: A council acknowledging a 'structural funding gap' is admitting its baseline spending commitments exceed its sustainable income. Zero-based budgeting across all services signals the scale of the gap is large enough to require examining every service from first principles rather than incremental savings. This is a material financial sustainability risk.
findings.figures: Zero-based budgeting exercise covering all council services; structural funding gap requiring multi-year strategy
findings.quote: zero-based budget review of all council services and identified of proposals that will enable a balanced budget to be set without recourse to reserves over the current medium term financial strategy

The improvement plan explicitly aimed to 'reduce reliance on reserves' as a core objective.
findings.matters: Reliance on reserves to balance revenue budgets is unsustainable and signals structural imbalance between income and spending. Reserves are finite; drawing them down reduces the council's financial buffer and signals worsening underlying financial position. Lenders assess reserve depletion as a key solvency risk.
