findings.headline: Head of Audit concludes control environment provides only 'Limited Assurance' despite improvement progress
findings.detail: The Head of Audit and Risk Management has concluded the Authority's control environment 'continues to provide Limited Assurance' (section 8.1-8.2). While acknowledging 'clear evidence of continued improvement' and noting it is 'too early to provide a Moderate Assurance opinion', the statement confirms the council remains below the standard assurance level. The Head of Audit has 'identified encouraging and measurable progress' but the overall assessment remains limited.
findings.matters: Limited assurance means material control weaknesses remain unresolved. This is a rating below normal standards and signals ongoing operational or financial risk that has not yet been remediated to acceptable levels.
findings.figures: Control environment rating: Limited Assurance (not Moderate); direction of travel noted as positive
findings.quote: the Authority's control environment continues to provide Limited Assurance. However, there is clear evidence of continued improvement across the Council's governance, risk management and internal control arrangements. Whilst it is considered too early to provide a Moderate Assurance opinion

findings.headline: Statutory audit recommendation from Forvis Mazars in December 2024 triggered formal governance overhaul
findings.detail: The council received a formal statutory recommendation from its external auditors in December 2024, indicating audit concerns about governance arrangements. The council responded with a structured Improvement Plan approved by Audit Committee on 9 January 2025, with progress monitored at every Audit Committee meeting throughout 2025-26. This represents a formal intervention level requiring active remediation.
findings.matters: Statutory recommendations from external auditors flag material governance or financial control weaknesses that lenders must factor into credit assessments. They indicate past failures and ongoing execution risk during remediation.
findings.figures: Recommendation issued December 2024; Improvement Plan approved 9 January 2025; progress reviewed at Audit Committee meetings on 8 April 2025, 23 July 2025, 20 October 2025, 8 December 2025 and 17 February 2026
findings.quote: The Council received a statutory recommendation from its Auditors in December 2024, the Council responded to the recommendations and prepared an Improvement Plan. The Plan was endorsed by Audit Committee at a Special meeting on the 9th of January 2025

findings.headline: Housing Repairs and Maintenance overspent by £1.792m (20.72%); disrepairs claims up 349% due to national trend
findings.detail: HRA Repairs and Maintenance overspent by £1.792m. Disrepairs claims (tenant claims against the council) jumped to £0.399m (349% overspend) due to a national trend of increasing litigation. Agency and specialist sub-contractor costs also overran. The paper notes this reflects 'both increased service demands and rising costs'.
findings.matters: Disrepairs liability is growing nationally and councils cannot easily control or forecast the volume or settlement value of claims. If this is a trend, HRA finances face upside cost risk that will eventually require reserve drawdown or rent rises.
findings.figures: £1.792m repairs overspend; £0.399m disrepairs overspend (349% of budget)
findings.quote: Disrepairs – there has been a national trend of increasing numbers of disrepair claims being made. The final overspend increased to £0.399m (349%), from a previously reported position at quarter 3 of broadly on budget.

findings.headline: DSG deficit now £20.285m (up from £19.041m); structural pressures persist after Project Safety Valve ends
findings.detail: The DSG deficit grew by £1.244m in 2025/26. Bury is under Project Safety Valve (which provides support until 2026/27), but the government's commitment to resolve 90% of the accrued deficit leaves the council liable for 10%. Underlying pressures are structural: HNB allocations not rising with pupil numbers, percentage of SEN pupils increasing, 19–25-year-olds added without funding, and reliance on expensive independent special school placements.
findings.matters: A £20m+ DSG deficit is not a cash problem today (grant covers it) but represents a future liability. When Safety Valve support ends, the council will need to either resolve the deficit against the grant or carry it as a non-cash reserve liability. Either way, it signals a structural mismatch in SEND provision.
findings.figures: DSG deficit £20.285m (up from £19.041m); increase of £1.244m in 2025/26
findings.quote: Bury Council operated under the Dedicated School Grant Safety Valve Intervention Programme during 2025/26 to address historic special education needs and disabilities (SEND) demand and cost pressures... Bury Council was due funding to support this work but this will now cease after 2025/26.

findings.headline: Collection Fund deficit of £2.223m driven by rising Council Tax arrears and collection rate fall to 95.26% (below pre-pandemic levels)
findings.detail: Council Tax collection fell to 95.26% against a 97.50% target—a 2.24 percentage point shortfall. The collection fund deficit was driven by increased bad debt provision due to rising arrears. The paper attributes this to 'cost-of-living pressures affecting residents'. Current collection rate (95.26%) remains below the pre-pandemic norm (96.39% in 2019/20).
findings.matters: Declining collection rates and rising arrears signal resident financial stress, which often precedes a broader economic downturn. This erodes a council's own revenue base independent of grant cuts and creates a dual squeeze: lower income + higher support demands.
findings.figures: £2.223m collection fund deficit; collection rate 95.26% vs 97.50% target; 2.24% shortfall
findings.quote: The in-year collection rate for Council Tax (95.26%) was below the budgeted collection rate (97.50%), a shortfall of 2.24%. This is largely due to the cost-of-living pressures affecting residents.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care recurring overspend of £2.696m mitigated by £0.800m one-off reserve use that 'does not address underlying cost pressures'
findings.detail: Care in the Community overspent by £5.186m (8%). One-off use of service reserves masked part of the problem. The paper explicitly states this reliance 'does not address the underlying cost pressures' and notes 'the scale of this overspend, together with the recurring nature of care costs, presents a significant risk to the service's 2026/27 opening budget position.'
findings.matters: Adult social care costs are structural and growing. Using one-off reserves to mask an overspend is a warning sign that the underlying cost base is not matched to budget, and the council is borrowing capacity from future years.
findings.figures: £2.696m HAC overspend; £5.186m Care in Community overspend; £0.800m one-off reserve mitigation
findings.quote: Although this has reduced the overall overspend reported within this budget, this reliance on one-off funding does not address the underlying cost pressures. The scale of this overspend, together with the recurring nature of care costs, presents a significant risk to the service's 2026/27 opening budget position.

findings.headline: Children and Young People overspend £5.491m (8.4%); residential placements 33.7% over budget with paper acknowledging 'challenge' to achieve 2026/27 savings
findings.detail: Residential placements overspent by £4.897m despite demand-reduction initiatives. The 2026/27 budget includes £5.984m growth to meet demand and inflation, offset by £4.711m in new savings targets. The paper states: 'It is anticipated that it will be a challenge to achieve the total savings target in year' and flags this as 'one of the continuing highest revenue risks to the council' requiring 'intensive oversight'.
findings.matters: Children's social care is typically a demand-led, price-inelastic cost that councils cannot easily cut. Overspends of this scale, combined with acknowledged difficulty achieving savings and continued demand pressures, represent a structural cost that will persist and likely grow, eroding the ability to balance the budget.
findings.figures: £5.491m directorate overspend; £4.897m residential placement overspend (33.7%); 10% reduction in resident placements in final quarter
findings.quote: It is anticipated that it will be a challenge to achieve the total savings target in year due to some of the savings related projects not fully in place, however the directorate are aiming to get the spends in this area and other placements in line with budget. The service acknowledges the risk and the area will be subject to detailed intensive oversight.

findings.headline: Structural £21m budget gap over MTFS to 2028/29 with no clear delivery plan
findings.detail: The council faces a cumulative £21m funding gap across the medium-term forecast to 2028/29. Work is 'being undertaken over the summer' to identify savings to address this, but no specific plan has been presented. The paper acknowledges both 'potential risks and opportunities' relating to demand and income variations, signalling uncertainty in the baseline assumptions.
findings.matters: A £21m structural deficit over three years — when combined with failed savings delivery, depleted reserves, and demand pressures in children's and adult services — suggests the council has not yet identified how it will balance its budget. This creates refinancing risk.
findings.figures: £21m forecast funding gap over MTFS; £13.898m gap for 2027/28 alone
findings.quote: Work is being undertaken over the summer to carry out a review of all budgets, in part informed by the outturn position, to identify savings to address the current c £21m forecast funding gap over the life of the current MTFS through to 2028/29.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves dropped to £44.106m (30.67% reduction in one year) and are now 'no longer sufficient' to cover forecast gaps
findings.detail: Reserves fell from £63.615m to £44.106m in a single year. The Budget Stabilisation Reserve specifically is projected to drop to £11.622m by March 2027 after £3.977m drawdown for 2026/27, while the council faces a £13.898m funding gap in 2027/28 alone. The paper explicitly states reserves 'no longer sufficient to support the forecast funding gap beyond 2027/28'.
findings.matters: Reserves are a council's shock absorber for unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls. When they fall below the level of forecast deficits, the council loses financial resilience and faces hard choices between cutting services, raising borrowing, or missing budgets.
findings.figures: Reserve balance fell £19.509m; BSR projected at £11.622m by March 2027 vs £13.898m gap in 2027/28
findings.quote: the reserve is no longer sufficient to support the forecast funding gap beyond 2027/28, however, work continues through the budget review of all services to identify saving proposals which will reduce the funding gap and reliance on reserves in future years.

findings.headline: Approved savings programme 31.81% undelivered: only £7.729m of £11.334m target achieved
findings.detail: The council's formal savings plan failed to deliver across the board. Two major slippages: £1.651m in Children and Young People (76% of their £2.116m target undelivered) and £2.160m in Non-Service Specific budgets (primarily the £1.610m Housing Integration saving). The paper notes delayed restructures and other implementation failures caused the underperformance.
findings.matters: A council's savings programme is the primary mechanism for addressing structural budget pressures. When 32% of approved savings don't materialise, it means the underlying deficit is larger than admitted and future recovery plans are unreliable.
findings.figures: £3.605m shortfall; £1.651m CYP failure; £1.610m Housing Integration failure
findings.quote: The Council's savings programme for 2026/27 totalled £11.334m, of which £7.729 (68.19%) has been delivered, a £1.094m adverse movement from quarter 3. The main reason for the underachievement is delayed implementation of restructures.

findings.headline: Council overspent £7.266m in 2025-26; total reserve drawdown £13.124m; paper states this "is not sustainable in the long term
findings.detail: The council overspent by £7.266m against a budget of £238.987m. This was in addition to £5.858m already budgeted to be drawn from the Budget Stabilisation Reserve, meaning total 2025/26 reserve drawdown was £13.124m. The paper explicitly states this drawdown 'is not sustainable in the long term' and signals this is the pattern across recent years with no clear correction path.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can fund its operations without continuous reserve depletion. Reserves are finite; sustained overspends signal structural problems that reserves cannot permanently solve.
findings.figures: £7.266m overspend; £13.124m total reserve drawdown in year; reserves fell £19.509m (30.67%)
findings.quote: To offset the overspend, a drawdown of £7.266m from the budget stabilisation reserve has been required. This has further reduced already low levels of reserves and is not sustainable in the long term.

findings.paper_title: Bury’s Local Area SEND Monitoring Inspection
findings.headline: Statutory override on DSG deficits ends 31st March 2028, with transition from Programme Safety Valve to interim Stability Grant
findings.detail: The council transitions from Programme Safety Valve support (which offsets the current deficit) to a High Needs Stability Grant for 2026-28. After 31st March 2028, when the statutory override ends, arrangements change to an unspecified new model. The paper notes this is a national challenge affecting an estimated £14-18 billion in unmitigated DSG deficits across England.
findings.matters: The ending of statutory protections and transition to an interim funding mechanism creates uncertainty about how DSG deficits will be managed after 2028, potentially affecting the council's financial position.
findings.figures: 31st March 2028 end date for statutory override; £14-£18 billion national unmitigated DSG deficit estimates
findings.quote: Bury council plans for the change from PSV to High Needs Stability Grant in 2026-28 for a two-year interim period whilst transitioning to the new model after the ending of the statutory override on 31st March 2028.

findings.paper_title: Bury’s Local Area SEND Monitoring Inspection
findings.headline: Bury's Dedicated School Grant High Needs block deficit stands at £20.285m as at 31st March 2026
findings.detail: SEND services continue to create pressure within the DSG High Needs block, which overspent by £5.462m in 2025-26. This overspend was offset by the Programme Safety Valve contribution and reserves, but the cumulative DSG deficit is now £20.285m—a material liability on the council's balance sheet.
findings.matters: A £20m+ deficit in a school funding block is a significant balance sheet liability that affects the council's financial position and creditworthiness for lending purposes.
findings.figures: £20.285m deficit as at 31 March 2026; £5.462m overspend in 2025-26
findings.quote: (High Needs block over-spent by £5.462m in 2025-26 before being offset by Programme Safety Valve (PSV) contribution and reserves released against the expenditure as agreed within the programme).  Bury DSG deficit balance as at 31st March 2026 is £20.285m.

findings.paper_title: GF Budget 2026-27 and MTFS 2027-29 Report -for Council FINAL 260217 (2)
findings.headline: Proposed parking and traffic enforcement income of £0.434m (2027/28) is draft, subject to consultation
findings.detail: The paper presents new income proposals from car parking, moving vehicle offences, and EV cross-pavement fees as a 'Policy Decision' requiring consultation. The £0.434m is included in the 2027/28 budget but explicitly noted as 'a prudent estimate' pending detailed work. If consultation fails or income falls short, 'the loss of forecast income would increase the forecast budget gap for 2027/28 and 2028/29.'
findings.matters: This represents £0.434m of unconfirmed savings in a budget already carrying a £21m unfunded gap. Any failure to deliver creates additional pressure in the hardest year of the MTFS (2027/28 has the largest incremental gap at £9.921m).
findings.figures: Proposed new income: £0.434m (2027/28); status: draft, subject to consultation; paper states savings are 'prudent estimate' pending delivery plans
findings.quote: The savings proposal in relation to potential additional income across 3 areas identified to be developed by the Place Directorate ; Parking; Moving Vehicle Offences and EV cross pavement fees totalling £0. 434m will be subject to a specific consultation process when fully developed proposals are brought forward to Cabinet in the new financial year

findings.paper_title: GF Budget 2026-27 and MTFS 2027-29 Report -for Council FINAL 260217 (2)
findings.headline: Use of £2m flexible capital receipts for revenue transformation in 2026/27 — a one-off funding source that is not available in future years
findings.detail: The budget relies on £2m of flexible capital receipts to fund Adults/Children's social care consultancy (Impower, £0.6m) and corporate transformation across finance, HR, digital, and procurement (£1.4m). This is not a sustainable funding source; it depletes capital and does not recur.
findings.matters: Flexible capital receipts funding is finite and crowds out capital investment in buildings, vehicles, and ICT. The council is using it to fund consultancy and transformation, not service delivery — a signal that reserves and revenue cannot bear these costs.
findings.figures: Flexible capital receipts for revenue: £2m (2026/27); allocation: Impower £0.6m, Procurement £0.4m, Finance £0.35m, HR £0.35m, Digital £0.3m
findings.quote: Flexible Use of Capital Receipts: the flexibility for councils to use capital receipts to be support revenue expenditure that delivers service transformation has been extended and £2m is included for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: GF Budget 2026-27 and MTFS 2027-29 Report -for Council FINAL 260217 (2)
findings.headline: Proposal to raise leisure subsidy reduction by 10% for three years (6% above inflation) to fund budget gap — subject to consultation but already included in budget
findings.detail: The paper includes £0.125m (2026/27), £0.155m (2027/28), £0.220m (2028/29) from 'Reduction of Leisure council subsidy.' Consultation showed majority support for modernisation but opposition to subsidy cuts. The council notes consultation 'outcomes will be considered by Cabinet' but has already built the savings into the budget.
findings.matters: Consultation feedback was mixed; public opposition to subsidy cuts is common. If the proposal fails to land after consultation, the council loses £0.5m+ of savings already counted, worsening the remaining gap.
findings.figures: Leisure subsidy reductions: £0.125m (2026/27), £0.155m (2027/28), £0.220m (2028/29); consultation showed 'mixed range of responses' with majority 'not in favour of reducing the overall budget'
findings.quote: The proposal put forward for consideration is recommending a price increase of 10% for 3 years (6% above inflation), which would equate to an increase of £3.25 per month for 2026/27

findings.paper_title: GF Budget 2026-27 and MTFS 2027-29 Report -for Council FINAL 260217 (2)
findings.headline: Heavy reliance on savings in Children's Looked After placements (£1.0m) based on a 'step-down plan' with no detail provided and existing demand growth offsetting assumed reductions
findings.detail: The budget assumes £1.0m of savings from 'reduction of residential placements' and demand reduction from Families First funding. However, the MTFS also assumes demand growth of 1.38%-2.28% in other children's social care areas (transition budgets, support at home). No phasing or mechanism is shown. The council is already £4.492m over on Children's Safeguarding in Q2; the plan to reduce placements sits against this reality.
findings.matters: Placement step-downs are difficult to execute — each placement is a child. Savings are easily displaced by one new complex case or delay in transitioning a young person. The offsetting demand growth suggests the council expects pressures to continue, making this £1m plan optimistic.
findings.figures: Children Looked After savings: £1.0m (single line item); Children's Safeguarding Q2 overspend £4.492m (9.05%); demand growth assumptions Children's Transition 1.49%-2.26%, other areas 1.38%-2.28%
findings.quote: Children Looked After Budgets: inflation (5%) and demand reduction based on a targeted child-by-child step down plan to reduce the number of residential placements

findings.paper_title: GF Budget 2026-27 and MTFS 2027-29 Report -for Council FINAL 260217 (2)
findings.headline: Council Tax base growth forecast at 0.02% in 2026/27, down from 1.46%, due to development viability issues — dampening the primary lever for funding growth
findings.detail: The paper attributes the 98% reduction in expected council tax base growth to 'current prevailing economic conditions impacting forecast completions resulting either in delays or projects deemed no longer viable.' The council assumes maximum permissible tax rises (2.99% general + 2% social care precept = 4.99%) but cannot rely on the traditional growth assumption that eases budget pressures over time.
findings.matters: Council Tax base growth has been the default pressure release valve. If regeneration and new housing are stalling, the council loses both the immediate income and the medium-term trajectory that makes long-term planning sustainable. Combined with funding disadvantage, this removes a key option.
findings.figures: Council tax base growth: 0.02% (2026/27), 0.75% (2027/28 and 2028/29), revised down from 1.46% forecast; council tax assumption: 4.99% annual increase (2.99% general + 2% social care precept)
findings.quote: The growth assumptions have reduced from 1.46% to 0.2% in 2026/27 due to current prevailing economic conditions impacting the forecast completions resulting either in delays or projects deemed no longer viable.

findings.paper_title: GF Budget 2026-27 and MTFS 2027-29 Report -for Council FINAL 260217 (2)
findings.headline: Bury receives £1,209.12 per capita funding vs Greater Manchester average of £1,330.88 — a structural disadvantage of £23.7m annually that cannot be closed locally
findings.detail: Under the Fair Funding Review 2.0, Bury is ranked 8th lowest funded among 10 GM authorities on a per-capita basis. The paper calculates an annual shortfall of £23.720m (compared to £13.766m in 2025/26), worsening materially. This is not a service delivery or management issue; it reflects the council's relative deprivation ranking and limited council tax base compared to neighbours.
findings.matters: This funding disadvantage is structural and will not change without government redistribution or Bury's deprivation profile improving. The council cannot generate £23.7m of additional income through charges or commercial activity. This forces a choice between reserve depletion or service cuts.
findings.figures: Bury CSP per head £1,209.12 vs GM average £1,330.88 (2026/27); annual shortfall if at GM average £23.720m; overall IMD rank 104 out of 296 nationally, 8th out of 10 GM authorities
findings.quote: If Bury received the average funding per head as its GM neighbours, it would benefit from an additional £23.720m per annum

findings.paper_title: GF Budget 2026-27 and MTFS 2027-29 Report -for Council FINAL 260217 (2)
findings.headline: Structural budget gap of £22.589m over three years cannot be closed by existing savings proposals; remaining gap of £21.155m requires new, untested measures
findings.detail: Approved savings proposals total £15.216m across the MTFS period. Even after these, a residual gap of £21.155m remains. The council has identified only £1.434m in new draft proposals (mostly operational, not yet consulted). The bulk of the three-year gap remains unfunded. The paper notes the S151 officer 'chairs a monthly finance board' focused on developing further proposals but provides no forward visibility of what these might be.
findings.matters: Unidentified savings of this magnitude (£21m+) with only three years to find them creates execution risk. Social care savings are notoriously difficult to deliver; the council has already commissioned external consultancy (Impower) at significant cost, suggesting internal plans are insufficient.
findings.figures: Total MTFS gap £22.589m; approved savings £15.216m; remaining unfunded gap £21.155m; new draft proposals £1.434m; Impower review cost £1.667m over three years
findings.quote: To continue to reduce the dependence on reserves and address the structural funding shortfall, it is critical that further savings, efficiencies or income generation are identified over the three-year MTFS period 2026/27 to 2028/29 to stabilise the Council's finances over the medium-term.

findings.paper_title: GF Budget 2026-27 and MTFS 2027-29 Report -for Council FINAL 260217 (2)
findings.headline: Q2 2025/26 overspend of £5.861m (2.45%) concentrated in Children's Safeguarding (£4.492m, 9.05%) and Adults Care in Community (£3.422m, 5.50%) — the exact services facing multi-year demand growth
findings.detail: Current-year outturn is running 2.45% over budget. The two worst-performing areas are Children's Safeguarding and Adults social care, where the MTFS assumes continuing demand growth of 0.62%-2.28% annually. In-year overspend of this magnitude directly depletes reserves and signals that demand assumptions in the MTFS may be optimistic.
findings.matters: Overspends in demand-driven services are sticky. If the council cannot absorb 2.45% variance this year, it is under-estimating the cost of meeting statutory obligations to vulnerable people. Any shortfall in demand reduction savings will accelerate reserve depletion.
findings.figures: Total forecast overspend £5.861m (2.45%); Children's £4.492m (9.05%); Adults £3.422m (5.50%). Demand growth assumptions: Adults Community Care 0.62%-2.28%, Adults Transition 1.49%-2.26%, Children CLA variable with step-down plan
findings.quote: The three main areas contributing to the £5.861m overspend are: Adults: the Care in the Community budget is forecast to overspend by £3.422m (5.50%). Children's: The Safeguarding and Social Care service budget is forecast to overspend by £4.492m (9.05%)

findings.paper_title: GF Budget 2026-27 and MTFS 2027-29 Report -for Council FINAL 260217 (2)
findings.headline: General Fund reserves fall to £0.294m by March 2029, breaching the £10m minimum holding and leaving no buffer for service pressures
findings.detail: Excluding statutory and ring-fenced reserves, usable reserves will contract from £53.615m in 2026 to £12.678m by 2029. The council proposes drawing £3.977m in 2026/27, £13.898m in 2027/28, and £21.155m in 2028/29 to cover budget gaps. The paper states: 'There are currently insufficient levels of reserves over the medium-term if there are no further efficiencies or savings proposals brought forward.'
findings.matters: A local authority at its reserve floor has no buffer for demand shocks, grant changes, or delivery delays on savings. This severely constrains borrowing capacity and refinancing flexibility.
findings.figures: General Fund reserves: £66.587m (2025) declining to -£0.294m (2029); budget stabilisation reserve draws: £3.977m, £13.898m, £21.155m across three years
findings.quote: There are currently insufficient levels of reserves over the medium-term if there are no further efficiencies or savings proposals brought forward.

findings.headline: The council holds £13m of LOBO loans with a 56.4% probability of refinancing at higher interest rates in April 2026.
findings.detail: Bury holds two £13m LOBO loans with refinancing options in 2026-27. The council assesses a 56.40% probability that one lender will exercise their option to propose an interest rate increase in April 2026. If exercised, the council states it will repay the loan to avoid refinancing risk in later years, but this represents a near-term refinancing event and potential cost increase.
findings.matters: For a lender, this refinancing risk represents a near-term event that could force the council to take action (repay) during a period when rates and market conditions are uncertain, and any increase in rates would further raise the council's debt service costs.
findings.figures: £13.000m LOBO loans; 56.40% probability of lender exercising option in April 2026
findings.quote: The Council holds two £13.000 million of Lender's Option Borrower's Option (LOBO) loans where the lender has the option to propose an increase in the interest rate as set dates, following which the Council has the option to either accept the new rate or to repay the loan at no additional cost. Both LOBO's have options during 2026/27 with a 56.40% probability of one of lenders exercising their option in April 2026.

findings.headline: Treasury investment balances are falling from £20.7m to £10m and are forecast to remain flat, indicating the council is drawing down its liquid resources.
findings.detail: The council explicitly states: 'Balances are lower than prior years due to internal borrowing levels. Balances are expected to fall further as borrowing held internally increases.' This means the council is using its investment reserves to cover capital expenditure rather than borrowing externally, which depletes the buffer available for cash management and unexpected needs.
findings.matters: For a lender, declining liquid reserves indicate the council has less financial flexibility to manage cash flow fluctuations or unexpected expenditure, increasing reliance on new borrowing.
findings.figures: Treasury investments: £20.700m (31 March 2025) declining to £10.000m (forecast 2026-27 and beyond)
findings.quote: During 2025/26 the Council's internal treasury investment balance has ranged between £20.000 million and £11.456 million. Balances are lower than prior years due to internal borrowing levels. Balances are expected to fall further as borrowing held internally increases.

findings.headline: Ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream for the General Fund is forecast to jump to 5.78% in 2026-27, an increase of 1.81 percentage points in a single year.
findings.detail: The council's General Fund financing costs (interest on debt and MRP) are forecast to rise from 3.97% of revenue in 2025-26 to 5.78% in 2026-27, and remain elevated at 5.43% and 5.53% in the following two years. The HRA shows a similar pattern: 9.06% rising to 11.58% in 2026-27. This means an increasing portion of the council's revenue budget is consumed by servicing existing debt, leaving less available for services.
findings.matters: For a lender, rising debt service ratios indicate the council's revenue is increasingly constrained by existing borrowing commitments, which affects its ability to borrow for future needs or weather revenue shocks.
findings.quote: Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream 2024-25 Actual £m 2025-26 Estimate £m 2026-27 Forecast £m ... GF 2.79% 3.97% 5.78%

findings.headline: Significant highways investment is conditional on GMCA approval and subject to government funding volatility
findings.detail: Of the £26.195m highways spend proposed for 2026-27, £14.228m (54%) is GMCA-directed funding for Mayor Challenge Fund, Active Travel Fund, Streets for All, and CRSTS schemes. These are subject to approval of business cases and design development. The paper notes 'expenditure is also reliant on further approval of developed plans', creating execution risk and limiting council control.
findings.matters: Over half the highways programme depends on external approval and volatile government grant funding, increasing the risk of programme delays or reductions if government priorities shift.
findings.figures: GMCA/TfGM directed schemes: £14.228m of £26.195m highways spend (54%); external funding total 2026-27: £48.589m of £110.212m capital spend (44%)
findings.quote: These are conditional grants and for programmes such as Highways the expenditure is also reliant on further approval of developed plans, thus ensuring the objectives set by GMCA are achieved

findings.headline: Council is using £2m of capital receipts to fund revenue spending on transformation, signalling revenue budget pressure
findings.detail: The 'Flexible Use of Capital Receipts' policy is being deployed to provide £2m for revenue spending in 2026-27, split across Adults/Children's Social Care (£0.6m), Procurement (£0.4m), Finance (£0.35m), HR (£0.35m), and digital (£0.3m). While framed as 'transformational activity', this represents capital being redirected to support day-to-day service costs.
findings.matters: Using non-recurring capital receipts to fund recurring revenue spending is a sign of structural revenue budget pressure and reduces non-recurring resources available for investment.
findings.figures: £2m flexible use of capital receipts for revenue: Adults & Children's Social Care £0.600m, Procurement £0.400m, Finance £0.350m, HR £0.350m, digital £0.300m
findings.quote: The flexibility for councils to use capital receipts to be support revenue expenditure that delivers service transformation has been extended and £2m is included for 2026/27. The £2m will be used to support the revenue budget and will be applied to Adults and Children's Social Care £0.600m, enabling services across the Corporate Core including Procurement £0.400m, Finance £0.350m, HR £0.350m and digital £0.300 m.

findings.headline: Council acknowledges capital receipts have not materialised as planned in past and relies on them despite the risk
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly identifies capital receipt delivery as 'a major risk and is one that has impacted on past programmes'. The council projects £3.035m of receipts in 2026-27 but applies risk-adjusted confidence levels (only 80% for 'high confidence' assets). Despite this history, the programme still depends on receipt realisation, creating execution risk.
findings.matters: A funding source with a documented history of underperformance remains central to the capital plan, increasing the risk of programme slippage or budget rebalancing mid-year.
findings.figures: Estimated receipts 2026-27: £3.035m (High confidence 80% adjustment: £0.859m; Medium 65%: £2.976m)
findings.quote: There is a risk that capital receipts are not realised to the level anticipated in the calculation of resources available to fund the capital programme. This is a major risk and is one that has impacted on past programmes.

findings.headline: Unit 4 system implementation needs an additional £1.1m and has faced integration problems
findings.detail: The council is requesting extra funding to complete the Unit 4 system upgrade beyond what was originally budgeted. The paper cites 'additional complexities resulting from the volume of integrating systems, coding complexities and gaps in process documentation' as reasons. This is being treated as necessary to 'ensure planned revenue savings are fully delivered', suggesting the system implementation is at risk of not delivering expected benefits.
findings.matters: System implementation failures directly threaten projected savings and can indicate underlying capability/governance weaknesses that affect other council operations and financial management.
findings.figures: Additional £1.1m required for Unit 4 upgrade
findings.quote: an additional £1.1m now required to complete the implementation of the Unit 4 system upgrade and address the additional complexities resulting from the volume of integrating systems, coding complexities and gaps in process documentation and ensure planned revenue savings are fully delivered

findings.headline: Borrowing costs will increase and add pressure to the revenue budget
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that borrowing will become a key source of financing the capital programme, with the Capital Financing Requirement growing from £464m to £512m over the planning period. The council's 2026/27 budget factors in borrowing costs, but anything beyond that will need to be included in future Medium-Term Financial Strategies, indicating uncertainty about affordability.
findings.matters: Growing debt servicing costs reduce financial flexibility and signal potential revenue budget stress ahead, which matters to lenders assessing long-term fiscal sustainability.
findings.figures: CFR growing from £464.113m (2025-26) to £511.995m (2028-29); Prudential Borrowing financing £30.361m of 2026/27 capital spend
findings.quote: borrowing will become a key source of financing, which will result in an increase in the cost of borrowing overall and will add pressure to the revenue budget

findings.headline: Finance transformation phase 2 is behind schedule, delaying improvements to financial governance and capacity
findings.detail: Finance Capacity and Transformation phase 2 was targeted for November 2025 but consultation begins 11 February 2026, several months late. This restructure is essential to addressing the auditors' findings on governance and financial sustainability and improving the council's capacity to manage finances.
findings.matters: Finance restructures required by audit findings indicate the council's current finance function is inadequate; delays mean audit-identified control weaknesses persist longer
findings.figures: Phase 2 originally due November 2025; consultation begins 11 February 2026 (status marked 'BEHIND')
findings.quote: The Phase Two consultation will begin on 11 February and complete in early March when any subsequent changes to the draft structure and approach to appointing will be confirmed.

findings.headline: The council faces an increasing funding gap in future years and continues to rely on reserves to balance budgets
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget reduces reserve drawdown through £14m in new proposals but still requires reserve support. The council explicitly acknowledges an 'increasing funding gap in future years' and must identify further proposals to eventually achieve a balanced budget without reserve use, indicating structural deficits beyond the current year.
findings.matters: Councils repeatedly drawing reserves to balance budgets are financially unsustainable; increasing gaps in the medium term signal structural problems rather than temporary pressures
findings.figures: £14m budget proposals considered; £7.5m funding gap at December 2025; reduced to under £4m in February 2026 budget
findings.quote: The revenue budget proposed f or 2026/27 includes a significantly lower contribution from re serves than in previous years but an increasing funding gap in future years within the current medium term financial strategy and therefore outlines the approach to be undertaken early in the new financial year to identify further proposals that will ultima tely enable a budget to set without recourse from reserves in future years.

findings.headline: External auditors issued a statutory recommendation after identifying three significant weaknesses in Value for Money arrangements
findings.detail: Forvis Mazars identified significant weaknesses across financial sustainability, governance, and economy/efficiency/effectiveness of services for 2021/22 and 2022/23. The council was formally required to develop a comprehensive improvement plan reflecting 'transformation and cultural change needed across all departments'.
findings.matters: Statutory audit recommendations indicate fundamental governance or financial control problems; lenders assess creditworthiness through audit findings and the need for external audit intervention is a red flag
findings.figures: Three significant weaknesses across all three reporting criteria; statutory recommendation issued 12 December 2024
findings.quote: They identified three significant weaknesses in the Council's arrangements. These weaknesses are across all three reporting cri teria that they are required to consider under the Code of Audit Practise, namely; financial sustainability, governance and for improving the economy, efficiency and effectiveness of services.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Bury Audit Strategy and Completion Report - Forvis Mazars
findings.headline: Budget setting for 2026/27 indicates continuing structural funding gap; council rejected some cost-reduction options proposed by members.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget setting process reflects that "Members have been presented with a range of options to both reduce costs and increase income but rejected some." Despite this, "the delivery of the savings plans that were agreed will be essential." The updated MTFS "shows a structural funding gap remain that needs to be addressed through the identification of new savings proposals for 2026/27." The 2025/26 budget proposals show "a budget gap after use of reserves of £16m (before savings proposals of 8.4m)."
findings.matters: A structural gap that persists despite intervention suggests the council has exhausted routine savings options. Rejecting some proposed reductions raises questions about whether remaining plans are realistic or if political resistance is blocking necessary action.
findings.figures: 2026/27 budget gap £16m (before £8.4m savings); structural gap persists
findings.quote: Members have been presented with a range of options to both reduce costs and increase income but rejected some. As a consequence, the delivery of the savings plans that were agreed will be essential.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Bury Audit Strategy and Completion Report - Forvis Mazars
findings.headline: Internal Audit opinion is Limited Assurance; 27 audit reviews yielded 165 recommendations, with concerns about implementation delays.
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit concluded: "Limited assurance could be given that significant risks facing the Council are addressed." 27 audits made 165 recommendations. 17 audits were still in progress at year-end. The opinion reflects "concerns about the high volume of limited assurance reports in the year, delays in the implementation of fundamental and significant recommendations and the ongoing governance and financial pressures." More recent governance arrangements (Governance Board) were introduced to improve implementation, but "it is too early to assess the effectiveness."
findings.matters: Limited assurance from internal audit is a red flag. The council is not addressing known control weaknesses, and recent interventions are too new to have proven effect.
findings.figures: 27 audits with 165 recommendations; 17 audits incomplete at year-end; Limited assurance opinion issued
findings.quote: The Head of Internal Audit concluded that Limited assurance could be given that significant risks facing the Council are addressed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Bury Audit Strategy and Completion Report - Forvis Mazars
findings.headline: Finance team lacks capacity, skills and experience to operate systems and controls; further restructure launched for 2025/26.
findings.detail: The auditor identifies that restructures in 2022 and 2023 left the council "without the capacity, skills and experience required to operate systems and processes as required to maintain an adequate system of internal control." Interim staff were used to bridge gaps at high cost. A further restructure and recruitment process was launched in 2025/26, alongside a planned financial systems upgrade.
findings.matters: Weak finance function means the council cannot reliably track its finances, identify problems, or manage cash. This is a root cause of the other failures identified.
findings.figures: Finance restructures in 2022 and 2023; further restructure and recruitment launched 2025/26
findings.quote: The changes left the Council without the capacity, skills and experience required to operate systems and processes as required to maintain an adequate system of internal control.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Bury Audit Strategy and Completion Report - Forvis Mazars
findings.headline: Three significant weaknesses in arrangements identified by the auditor; audit team struggled to get timely responses from council.
findings.detail: The auditor identified 3 significant weaknesses in Value for Money arrangements (across financial sustainability, governance, and other areas). The auditor notes: "we have struggled to secure timely engagement following our requests for information and meetings. At times, we have faced significant delays in receiving information. We remain concerned about the Council's ability to support our work in future years." The auditor was unable to complete audit walkthroughs for children's social care due to difficulty securing officer time.
findings.matters: Difficulty engaging with auditors indicates either lack of resources or lack of priority given to financial accountability. The council's ability to rebuild assurance is questioned by its own auditor.
findings.figures: 3 significant weaknesses in arrangements identified; walkthroughs not completed for children's social care
findings.quote: However, as in previous years, and despite the full co-operation of Executive Leadership, we have struggled to secure timely engagement following our requests for information and meetings.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Bury Audit Strategy and Completion Report - Forvis Mazars
findings.headline: Financial statements published four months late (October 2025 vs 30 June deadline); Annual Governance Statement was poorly drafted with errors.
findings.detail: The 2024/25 draft financial statements should have been published by 30 June 2025 but were not published until October 2025. The supporting Annual Governance Statement was poor quality: "a poorly drafted document containing typographical errors, references to the wrong year and hyperlinks to documents that did not work." The auditor reported this in November 2025 but had not received a revised draft at time of this report.
findings.matters: Late, poor-quality financial reporting delays decision-making by members, stakeholders, and creditors. It indicates either understaffing, lack of competence, or systemic chaos in the finance and governance function.
findings.figures: 4-month delay in accounts publication (30 June to October 2025); AGS not revised as of report date (Feb 2026 meeting date)
findings.quote: The Council's 2024/25 draft financial statements were due for publication by the statutory deadline of 30 June 2025. However, the accounts were late and were not published on the Council's website until October 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Bury Audit Strategy and Completion Report - Forvis Mazars
findings.headline: Capital programme was cut by more than half in-year, from £170.3m approved to £79.17m spent.
findings.detail: The council approved a 2024/25 capital programme of £146.92m in February 2024, which was increased by £23.42m to £170.347m to accommodate slippage. However, subsequent in-year reviews reduced the programme to just £79.17m spent. This suggests severe difficulties in delivering capital plans.
findings.matters: Inability to deliver approved capital programmes indicates weak planning, project management, or underlying financial stress. It suggests the council approved a capital budget it cannot actually deliver.
findings.figures: Approved budget Feb 2024: £146.92m; increased to £170.347m; actual spend £59.81m; final planned programme £79.17m
findings.quote: However, subsequent in-year capital programme reviews led to the 2024/25 capital programme being reduced to £79.17m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Bury Audit Strategy and Completion Report - Forvis Mazars
findings.headline: Borrowings increased £30m in 12 months to March 2025, largely for capital spending.
findings.detail: The council's borrowings increased by £30m over the 12-month period to 31/03/2025. This is stated to be largely to fund the capital programme. Cash position remains low at £1.2m (increased £0.7m from prior year). The Minimum Revenue Provision charge of £3.2m spreads capital financing over approximately 117 years, which the auditor notes "may not be sufficiently prudent."
findings.matters: Increasing debt while reserves fall is unsustainable. The auditor's concern about MRP prudence suggests the council may not be adequately charging for capital spending, masking the true cost of its capital programme.
findings.figures: Borrowings increased £30m in 12 months; cash balance £1.2m; MRP charge £3.2m (2024/25) vs £2.5m (2023/24); capital financing spread over ~117 years
findings.quote: borrowings have increased by £30m over the twelve-month period to 31/03/2025, largely to fund the capital programme.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Bury Audit Strategy and Completion Report - Forvis Mazars
findings.headline: OFSTED inspection in May 2024 identified "widespread and/or systemic failings" in SEND services
findings.detail: OFSTED's May 2024 inspection of SEND services concluded there were "widespread and/or systemic failings leading to significant concerns about the experiences and outcomes of children and young people with special educational needs and/or disabilities." The DfE is monitoring closely. It is noted that "it is too early to determine the impact of these actions."
findings.matters: SEND failures drive much of the DSG deficit overspend. DfE involvement means the council is under heightened regulatory oversight. Service failures can trigger intervention that constrains the council's financial autonomy.
findings.figures: OFSTED inspection May 2024; DSG deficit related to need for costly Independent and Non-Maintained Special School (INMSS) provision
findings.quote: In May 2024 OFSTED published the results of its inspection of the Council's SEND services. This inspection concluded there were widespread and/or systemic failings leading to significant concerns about the experiences and outcomes of children and young people with special educational needs and/or disabilities (SEND).

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Bury Audit Strategy and Completion Report - Forvis Mazars
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £19.04m and rising, with Safety Valve agreement behind schedule.
findings.detail: The DSG deficit stands at £19.04m in the draft 2024/25 accounts. The council's Safety Valve agreement with DfE, meant to eradicate the deficit by end of 2024/25, has not been met. The agreement was revised to target eradication by end of 2028/29. The 2025/26 projection shows the deficit rising to £21.5m with a £2.5m overspend.
findings.matters: The DSG deficit is unfunded and cannot be addressed through reserves. Rising deficits in children's services reflect both demand pressures and service failures (see SEND OFSTED outcome). This constrains the council's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £19.04m DSG deficit (2024/25); projected £21.5m (2025/26); revised Safety Valve timeline to 2028/29 (was 2024/25)
findings.quote: The deficit stands at £19.04m as presented in the draft 2024/25 statements. Although the Council entered into a Safety Valve agreement with the Department for Education (DfE) in 2021, intended to eradicate the DSG deficit by the end of the 2024-25, the Council has not been able to do so.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Bury Audit Strategy and Completion Report - Forvis Mazars
findings.headline: Council incurred £4.365m revenue overspend in 2024/25 despite setting a balanced budget.
findings.detail: The council approved a balanced budget for 2024/25 with reliance on £15.1m reserves and £5.3m savings. It still overspent by £4.365m on a final revised budget of £224.480m. Health & Adult Care and Children and Young People services alone reported overspends of £3.7m and £2.5m respectively.
findings.matters: The council is consistently unable to remain within budget. This pattern suggests either uncontrolled service demand, inadequate cost control, or budgets that do not reflect operational reality.
findings.figures: £4.365m overspend on £224.480m budget; Health & Adult Care £3.7m overspend; Children and Young People £2.5m overspend; 2024/25 approved budget relied on £15.1m reserves
findings.quote: The Council reported a final overspend on the revenue budget of £4.365m for 2024/35 on a final revised budget of £224.480m. A significant amount of the overspend relates to Health & Adult Care and Children and Young People services which reported a £3.7m and 2.5 overspend.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Bury Audit Strategy and Completion Report - Forvis Mazars
findings.headline: General Fund reserves fell £28m in one year and are now insufficient to cover forecast funding gaps.
findings.detail: Usable reserves declined significantly from £99.6m (31 Mar 2024) to £71.57m (31 Mar 2025). The Budget Stabilisation Reserve is explicitly noted as insufficient to support the funding gap forecast past 2026/27. The council's reliance on reserves to balance budgets is unsustainable.
findings.matters: Falling reserves reduce the council's financial resilience. A lender needs to know whether the council can manage a service shock or revenue shortfall without breaching statutory controls.
findings.figures: Reserves fell £28m in 12 months; General Fund fell from £99.6m to £71.57m; Budget Stabilisation Reserve now insufficient beyond 2026/27
findings.quote: General Fund and earmarked reserves reduced by £28 m, from £99.6 (31 Mar 2024) to £71.57m (31 Mar 2025). The Budget Stabilisation Reserve is now insufficient to support the funding gap forecast past 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Bury Audit Strategy and Completion Report - Forvis Mazars
findings.headline: Council declared itself in financial distress in summer 2024 and has failed to stabilise despite intervention.
findings.detail: The council declared financial distress and established a Financial Improvement Panel with CIPFA and LGA support. Despite this, the auditor found the council "did not have a clear understanding of its financial position or of the Council's cost base." A new Section 151 officer was appointed (interim, then substantive). The budget for 2025/26 still required £5.8m from reserves to balance, and the forecast shows continuing overspends.
findings.matters: Financial distress declaration signals systemic inability to manage within budget. The auditor's finding that leadership lacked basic understanding of financial position indicates control failures at the highest level.
findings.figures: Summer 2024 distress declaration; £5.8m reserves used for 2025/26 budget; forecast overspend of £4.15m in Q1 2025/26
findings.quote: In the summer of 2024, the Council declared itself to be in a state of financial distress.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Bury Audit Strategy and Completion Report - Forvis Mazars
findings.headline: Auditor cannot verify the 2024/25 accounts due to insufficient procedures before the statutory backstop date.
findings.detail: The external auditor will issue a disclaimed opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements, meaning no assurance is provided. The auditor states: "It has not been possible to complete sufficient procedures as part of the current year's audit to enable us to issue a non-disclaimed opinion." This follows disclaimed opinions in 2021/22, 2022/23 and 2023/24, creating a four-year gap in verified accounts.
findings.matters: A lender cannot verify what the council's actual financial position is. Without verified accounts, the council's reported reserves, debt, and solvency position are unaudited.
findings.figures: Four consecutive years of disclaimed opinions: 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25
findings.quote: It has not been possible to complete sufficient procedures as part of the current year's audit to enable us to issue a non-disclaimed opinion.

findings.headline: Prolonged underfunding of maintenance creates risk of major future cost escalation when structural layers fail
findings.detail: The plan explicitly warns that deferring capital maintenance beyond certain thresholds allows assets to deteriorate to the point where cost-effective repair is no longer possible. When underlying structural layers are compromised, full reconstruction becomes necessary at significantly higher cost. This creates a latent financial obligation that could force emergency capital spending in future years.
findings.matters: For a council holding a £1.273bn asset, this is a documented financial risk: today's maintenance savings create tomorrow's unplanned capital obligations. A lender assessing long-term debt serviceability needs to understand whether the council is accepting this deferred-cost scenario deliberately or whether future budgets will be available to prevent it.
findings.figures: £1.273 billion asset value; optimal annual maintenance £9.5m
findings.quote: A key risk associated with prolonged underfunding of capital maintenance is that assets deteriorate beyond the point where cost-effective, whole-life interventions are feasible. For carriageway and footway pavement assets, this can result in the degradation of underlying structural layers, which typically have a longer design life than surface treatments. Once compromised, these layers may require full reconstruction, significantly increasing costs.

findings.headline: Annual highway maintenance requires £9.5m but capital budget falls from £7.7m to £4.5m in 2026/27 after Highway Investment Strategy ends
findings.detail: The plan documents that optimal annual maintenance of Bury's carriageway network requires £9.5 million. Actual capital budgets are £8.138m (2023/24), £7.695m (2024/25), £7.695m (2025/26), and £4.528m (2026/27). The 2026/27 drop reflects the end of the Highway Investment Strategy (HIS) supplementary funding, which has added £3.167m annually through 2025/26.
findings.matters: Bury holds a £1.273bn highway asset but is accepting budgets below the documented optimal maintenance level, creating risk of accelerated asset deterioration and future cost escalation. A finance director or lender needs to understand whether this underfunding is planned, sustainable, or signals future pressure.
findings.figures: £9.5 million optimal annual requirement; actual budgets: £8,138k (2023/24), £7,695k (2024/25), £7,695k (2025/26), £4,528k (2026/27)
findings.quote: For Bury's carriageway network, the optimal maintenance strategy—based on current lifecycle modelling and treatment assumptions—has been calculated to require an annualised average investment of £9.5 million.

findings.headline: Approval of the Highway Asset Management Plan is required to remain eligible for 25% of a £500 million government funding allocation
findings.detail: The government has made a portion of highway maintenance funding contingent on councils adopting best practice asset management. The council seeks Cabinet approval for its Highway Asset Management Plan to remain eligible. Without it, Bury risks losing access to a portion of available government highway funding.
findings.matters: Access to government capital funding is critical for maintaining the council's £1.2 billion highway asset; loss of eligibility would require the council to fund maintenance from its own resources
findings.figures: 25% of a £500 million UK local highway maintenance fund; highway assets valued at approximately £1.2 billion on a Gross Replacement Cost basis
findings.quote: This year, the Government announced that 25% of a £500 million UK local highway maintenance fund for 2025 to 2026 is contingent on us demonstrating that we are using best practice asset management practice.

findings.headline: New MRP legislation from April 2024 will require significantly higher minimum revenue provisions from 2025/26 onwards, and capital receipts can no longer offset MRP charges.
findings.detail: Amended MRP regulations published 10 April 2024 take effect from 2025/26, requiring councils to charge higher minimum revenue provision on capital loans given after 7 May 2024. Capital receipts are no longer permitted to replace or offset the prudent MRP charge (except in limited circumstances). These regulatory changes increase the council's required annual revenue spending and reduce flexibility in managing budgets for competing priorities.
findings.matters: New regulatory costs will increase the council's annual budget requirement from 2025/26, reducing financial flexibility and potentially constraining funding available for services or unforeseen pressures.
findings.figures: Changes effective 2025/26; apply to capital loans issued from 7 May 2024 onwards
findings.quote: On 10 April 2024 amended legislation and revised statutory guidance were published on Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP). The majority of the changes take effect from the 2025/26 financial year, although there is a requirement that for capital loans given on or after 7th May 2024 sufficient MRP must be charged

findings.headline: The council holds £66.2m in non-treasury commercial and property investments, concentrated in Manchester Airport (£35m) and Bury town-centre regeneration schemes.
findings.detail: Non-treasury investments total £66.222m, with major exposures to property and commercial development: Manchester Airport (£5.610m equity plus £29.366m loan), Bury Bruntwood Millgate town-centre regeneration (£20.099m), Townside Fields (£7.257m), and Prestwich regeneration (£1.127m). These represent substantial bets on property valuations and project completion in a challenging real estate environment. The Manchester Airport exposure of £35m is particularly material for a single council.
findings.matters: Concentrated exposure to property and regeneration projects carries completion and valuation risk; if schemes stall or property valuations fall, these assets could become impaired, reducing balance sheet resilience.

findings.quote: Manchester Airport Equity £5.610 Manchester Airport Loan £29.366 Bury MBC Townside Fields Loan £7.257 Bury Bruntwood (Millgate) LLP Loan £20.099

findings.detail: Non-HRA capital expenditure outturn was £43.511m against revised budget of £61.517m, despite the original February 2024 budget having been £123.846m — a 47% downward revision in one year followed by a further 29% variance to actual. The council attributes this to 'expenditure rephasing' (project delays). This scale of slippage affects the council's ability to deliver planned capital schemes and may create delays in intended service improvements and asset replacements.
findings.matters: Large capital programme variances and rephasing indicate either delivery challenges, declining demand, or fundamental changes to investment plans, affecting both revenue impact and the timeline for intended improvements.

news_drafts.headline: Bury faces £9.585m gap in 2027/28 budget after £10.747m of proposed savings
news_drafts.lead:
Bury Council's Cabinet on 14 October is presented with a refreshed medium-term financial strategy (MTFS, the council's multi-year plan setting expected spending against expected income). It shows a gap of £20.332m for 2027/28 before savings. The council proposes £10.747m of new savings, mainly by deleting vacant posts, redesigning services and changing policies. That leaves £9.585m, rising to a cumulative £17.508m by 2029/30.

The 2027/28 gap is £6.434m larger than the £13.898m set when the budget was approved in February 2026. Budget assumptions rose by £6.161m and expected funding fell by £0.273m. Demand and volume growth adds £4.084m, treasury and capital financing costs £3.094m, and the 6.4% rise in the Real Living Wage (the voluntary hourly pay rate set above the legal minimum) £1.482m. In-year budget monitoring (the check of spending against budget) forecasts a 2026/27 overspend of £5.691m, or 2.26% of the £252.135m net budget. Health and Adult Care accounts for £2.543m and Children and Young People £2.212m.

Money set aside to support the budget, the Budget Stabilisation Reserve, is forecast to fall from £15.599m at March 2026 to £5.977m at March 2027. That follows £3.977m of approved use this year and an estimated £5.691m to cover the overspend. The paper states: "The Council no longer has a sufficient Budget Stabilisation Reserve to fund the current budget gaps and therefore cannot rely upon reserves as a viable means of balancing future budgets."
